tldr: MMUSV-Sim is a UE5-based simulation and data-generation platform designed for researching cooperative perception across multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs). It realistically reproduces wave-induced vessel motion and blind spots, demonstrating that multi-agent cooperation dramatically boosts detection accuracy for distant and occluded vessels from 45.54% (single USV) to 72.74%.
hero_caption: A typical cooperative perception scenario addressed by MMUSV-Sim. The target vessel (a large cargo ship) is occluded by an island from the perspective of USV 1 in the foreground. By integrating observation data from USV 2 and USV 3 at different viewing angles into a shared Bird's-Eye View (BEV) coordinate system, the blind spot is eliminated and the target is accurately captured.
overview:
Unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) are increasingly deployed for harbor patrol and maritime traffic monitoring. However, relying on a single vessel's sensors always carries the risk of missing targets hidden behind islands, port structures, or other ships. Cooperative perception—where multiple USVs share and pool their sensor data—offers a promising solution. Yet researching this solely through real-world maritime experiments is extremely costly and difficult due to the challenges of procuring multiple vessels, synchronizing sensors, and providing accurate 3D annotations. While simulators exist for autonomous vehicles, they cannot reproduce maritime-specific wave motions, extreme scale variations ranging from a few meters to hundreds of meters, or complex occlusions caused by landmasses and islands.

To address this gap, the authors developed MMUSV-Sim, a perception-oriented simulation platform built on Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) and Project AirSim. It provides three core environments—island, open-sea, and port—with flexible control over weather, time of day, and wave conditions. It also enables straightforward generation of synchronized multimodal observation data across cameras, LiDAR, and radar. Furthermore, vessel motions such as pitch and roll induced by waves are synthesized from physical parameters.

Experiments confirmed that vessel attitude changes respond as intended to configured wave settings, and that geometric consistency between generated annotations and renderings is well preserved. Furthermore, on a LiDAR-based cooperative bird's-eye view (BEV) vessel detection benchmark using the generated data, Early Fusion achieved an AP@0.5 of 72.74 compared to 45.54 with a single vessel (No Fusion). Evaluating robustness against communication delays and localization errors, MMUSV-Sim establishes a solid foundation for maritime cooperative perception research.
contributions: Built a UE5-based simulation platform specialized for maritime cooperative perception, featuring island, open-sea, and port environments, over 30 vessel assets, and configurable waves and weather.

Implemented a consistent data collection and annotation export pipeline that pauses scene progression to perfectly align multimodal sensor observations with ground-truth world states across all agents.
Proposed a perception-oriented vessel motion model combining smooth spline-based trajectories with realistic heave, roll, and pitch perturbations scaled by wave conditions and vessel dimensions.

Constructed an OPV2V-compatible dataset and conducted a cooperative BEV object detection benchmark, thoroughly quantifying the advantages of Early Fusion as well as the impacts of communication latency and localization errors.

sections.heading: Why do we need a maritime cooperative perception simulator?
sections.summary: A single USV faces severe sensing range limits and blind spots that multi-USV cooperative perception can overcome. However, real-world multi-agent maritime trials are prohibitively difficult, and existing maritime simulators were not designed for perception data generation. To solve this, the authors proposed MMUSV-Sim.
sections.details:
For autonomous navigation and harbor surveillance at sea, accurately detecting surrounding vessels is the cornerstone of safety. However, sensors mounted on a single USV (marine drone) suffer from limited sensing ranges and narrow fields of view, along with significant occlusions caused by islands, coastal terrain, port infrastructure, and large vessels. Cooperative perception, where multiple vessels share complementary observations, is expected to solve these issues.

However, building datasets by deploying multiple vessels in real waters is a daunting undertaking. Procuring multiple boats, calibrating sensors, staffing operators, and managing weather and navigational safety incur tremendous costs and operational constraints. Most existing open maritime datasets (such as MaSTr1325 and SeePerSea) remain limited to single-vessel perspectives, making multi-vessel synchronized data extremely scarce.

While cooperative simulators like CARLA and OPV2V have achieved great success in autonomous driving and UAV domains, they cannot be directly transferred to maritime settings. The maritime domain features expansive open-water layouts, occlusions from islands and harbors, extreme scale discrepancies from small multi-meter boats to several-hundred-meter cargo ships, and, above all, vessel attitude perturbations caused by waves. Furthermore, conventional marine robotics simulators mainly focus on control and hydrodynamic fidelity rather than serving as data pipelines for training and evaluating cooperative perception algorithms. This motivated the authors to develop MMUSV-Sim, an integrated platform focused specifically on perception research.

sections.heading: System architecture of MMUSV-Sim: from scenario setup to data export
sections.summary: Combining UE5 and Project AirSim, the platform streamlines scenario configuration, sensor acquisition, and annotation generation. Key features include dual manual and rule-based batch generation modes, a wave- and vessel-scale-aware motion model, and a simulation-pause protocol that guarantees perfect synchronization across all vessels.
sections.details:
MMUSV-Sim comprises three core components: a scenario configuration module, a UE5-based simulation engine, and an orchestration and data-generation interface. The overall workflow executes configured scenarios in UE5, records multimodal observations alongside a shared world state, and exports per-agent annotations offline.

### II-A UE5-Based Simulation Engine
Using high-fidelity Unreal Engine 5 as its rendering backbone, the system features three representative environments: Island, Open sea, and Port. Parameters provide flexible control over time of day, weather, illumination, and wave intensity. The asset library includes over 30 vessel types, ranging from ~3 m speedboats to ~300 m container ships. Each USV can be equipped via Project AirSim with panoramic RGB cameras, depth cameras, semantic segmentation cameras, BEV top-view cameras, panoramic LiDAR, and ray-tracing-based marine radar.

### II-B Scenario Configuration and Orchestration
Scenarios can be created in two ways. One is an interactive mode using a graphical Bird's-Eye View (BEV) interface to manually configure vessel placements, spline trajectories, and weather conditions. The other is a batch-generation mode that automatically samples numerous feasible scenarios given difficulty parameters, vessel counts, and layout rules. The batch generator validates geometric constraints including water masks, land clearance margins, sensing ranges, inter-vessel distances, and occlusion conditions, exporting only valid configurations.

### II-C Perception-Oriented Vessel Motion Model
Because strict hydrodynamic simulation is computationally heavy, the authors adopted a smart motion model tailored to the attitude variations necessary for perception evaluation. Base vessel transit is computed as smooth forward motion along a spline curve $\mathbf{c}_v(d)$, upon which localized perturbations in heave, roll, and pitch driven by wave parameters are superimposed. A vessel-volume scaling factor $\alpha_v$ attenuates perturbations for larger vessels, realistically reproducing intuitive behaviors where small boats rock vigorously while large ships remain steady.

### II-D Multi-USV Data Acquisition and Export
The most notable design choice in data recording is pausing the simulation. At a fixed acquisition frequency $f$ (period $\Delta t = 1/f$), the physics tick is paused to update buffers and simultaneously capture camera, LiDAR, and radar streams across all USVs. This yields perfectly synchronized observations and ground-truth world states without millisecond-level offsets. Captured data is then transformed into each USV's local coordinate frame, automatically exporting 2D/3D bounding boxes, BEV boxes, and radar PPI images in an OPV2V-compatible format.

sections.heading: Experiments: wave perturbation verification, geometric consistency, and cooperative BEV detection
sections.summary: After verifying wave-driven vessel attitude perturbations and annotation geometric consistency, a LiDAR cooperative BEV detection benchmark was conducted on the generated dataset. Early Fusion achieved an AP@0.5 of 72.74, greatly outperforming single-USV detection (45.54), and its robustness against communication delays and localization noise was evaluated.
sections.details:
The experiments consisted of three parts: attitude perturbation verification under wave settings, geometric consistency evaluation of annotations and renderings, and LiDAR cooperative BEV detection benchmark evaluation. The detection benchmark utilized 41 sequences (3,129 frames total) across island, open-sea, and port environments, partitioned into 32 training sequences (2,463 frames) and 9 test sequences (666 frames).

### III-A Controllable Attitude Perturbation Verification
Vessel motion response was evaluated across stepped wave height settings: W0 (0–1 m), W1 (1–2 m), W2 (2–3 m), and W3 (3–4 m). The root-mean-square (RMS) of heave increased monotonically from 0.013 m to 0.307 m, roll from 0.183° to 4.048°, and pitch from 0.091° to 2.189°. This demonstrated that wave configurations effectively produce intended sensor attitude perturbations.

### III-B Geometric Consistency of Annotations and Renderings
The convex hull $H_{\mathrm{proj}}$ obtained by projecting 3D bounding boxes onto a top-view camera was compared against the semantic vessel mask $M_{\mathrm{local}}$. Across 10,354 projected target vessels, the median center error was just 2.08 pixels, and the mask inclusion ratio (how well the rendered vessel fits inside the bounding box) averaged an extremely high 0.999 (99.9%). The average occupancy ratio was 0.424, reflecting the natural empty space between a rectangular 3D box and actual vessel hull contours, thereby confirming the precision of the geometric pipeline.

### III-C LiDAR Cooperative BEV Detection Benchmark
Vessel detection was evaluated on 64-beam LiDAR data using a detector combining PointPillars and CenterPoint. Three configurations were compared:
- **No Fusion**: Baseline using only the ego USV's LiDAR
- **Late Fusion**: Aggregating bounding boxes independently detected by each USV into the ego frame and applying NMS
- **Early Fusion**: Aggregating raw point clouds from all USVs into the ego frame before feeding them to the detector

The results were dramatic. In an ideal setting (zero communication delay and zero localization error), No Fusion scored an AP@0.5 of 45.54, while Late Fusion reached 55.47 and Early Fusion achieved 72.74. In distant ranges (150–200 m), Early Fusion reached an AP@0.5 of 68.04, more than doubling No Fusion's 31.22.

Stress testing was also conducted under realistic operational constraints. Under communication latency (200–600 ms), Early Fusion retained an AP@0.5 of 58.06 at 600 ms delay, maintaining a 12.52-point advantage over No Fusion. Conversely, 6-DoF localization noise posed a severe challenge: while AP@0.5 remained at 63.64 under 0.5 m / 0.5° noise, increasing noise to 2.0 m / 2.0° caused Early Fusion to plummet to 25.17 and Late Fusion to 28.95, both dropping below the single-vessel (No Fusion) baseline. This highlights a critical real-world challenge: when spatial misalignments are large, directly merging point clouds causes blurry, duplicated artifacts that make Early Fusion even more vulnerable than Late Fusion.

captions.F6: Qualitative comparison in a port scenario. Red boxes represent ground truth (GT), and blue boxes represent predictions. For large ships docked along the wharf, No Fusion and Late Fusion produce multiple misoriented boxes due to partial views. In contrast, Early Fusion aggregates multi-view point clouds to reveal the complete vessel geometry, matching the GT cleanly.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: MMUSV-Sim delivers a high-precision simulation and data generation environment for maritime cooperative perception. The platform demonstrated controllable wave-induced motions and annotation accuracy, proved that cooperative detection significantly outperforms single-vessel sensing, and highlighted localization error compensation as a key research direction.
sections.details:
This paper presented MMUSV-Sim, a simulation and data-generation platform designed to advance multi-USV cooperative perception research. Built on UE5, it integrates diverse topologies (ports, open sea, islands), weather and wave controls, over 30 vessel assets, and a consistent data collection protocol.

Experiments confirmed that wave-induced attitude dynamics are faithfully reproduced and that annotation projections from world to sensor coordinates maintain high geometric consistency. Furthermore, on a LiDAR cooperative BEV detection benchmark, Early Fusion combining multi-USV data substantially improved AP@0.5 from 45.54 to 72.74 over single-USV sensing.

The benchmark also quantified the impact of communication latency and localization errors inevitable in real-world maritime operations. In particular, attitude estimation errors exacerbated by rough sea states severely degrade Early Fusion performance, pointing to robust feature fusion and pose correction algorithms as critical areas for future work. MMUSV-Sim provides a highly valuable testbed for developing and validating next-generation maritime cooperative autonomous systems.

takeaways: Early Fusion integrating multi-USV observations dramatically improves BEV detection accuracy for distant and occluded vessels compared to single-USV perception (AP@0.5: 45.54 → 72.74).

While cooperative gains remain resilient against communication latency (up to 600 ms), severe localization errors (2 m / 2° or higher) lead to performance degradation where cooperation performs worse than single-USV sensing.
MMUSV-Sim employs a scene-pause data acquisition protocol, enabling large-scale generation of multimodal, multi-agent data with perfect millisecond-level synchronization and ground-truth annotations.
limitations: Rather than simulating rigorous fluid-structure hydrodynamics between waves and hulls, wave-induced perturbations are geometrically synthesized using periodic functions scaled by wave height.
The cooperative detection benchmark was evaluated exclusively on LiDAR-based single-class (vessel) detection, leaving cross-modal cooperative perception combining cameras and radar for future work.
Direct verification of the Sim-to-Real gap against physical datasets collected from actual vessels in real maritime environments was not included.
